newsitem.title: USA: Financier Hoffenberg to get 20-year sentence.
newsitem.headline: Financier Hoffenberg to get 20-year sentence.

text.p: A federal judge plans to sentence financier Steven Hoffenberg, accused of masterminding the biggest financial swindle in U.S. history, to 20 years in prison and order him to pay $476 million in restitution.
U.S. District Judge Robert Sweet said in an opinion made public Wednesday that he plans to sentence Hoffenberg on Friday for causing thousands of victims to lose half a billion dollars.
"Here, an unstable individual with manic tendencies and a sense of grandiosity violated the law in order to satisfy his own greed and sense of entitlement," Sweet said.

Hoffenberg, 52, had headed Towers Financial Corp., the bill-collection business that filed for bankruptcy protection from creditors in 1993 after it was discovered that the flamboyant financier was using the company to operate what prosecutors called the largest Ponzi scheme ever in the United States.
Hoffenberg, who gained attention when he offered to rescue the New York Post in January 1993, pleaded guilty to conspiracy and fraud charges in April 1995.
He recently asked to withdraw the plea, claiming he was mentally unfit when he admitted to the fraud.

Sweet denied his request but said Hoffenberg has a history of mental illness dating back to a hospitalization in 1970 that included electroconvulsive therapy, anti-psychotic medications and a mood stablizer. As recently as March 1995 he was diagnosed as having a mixed personality disorder and had been placed on anti-depressant medications.

The judge said Hoffenberg suffers from a condition "that from time to time has limited his ability to perceive reality accurately." However, he said Hoffenberg has known of his condition since 1970 and has had the resources to "manage" and "cope" with it and is responsible for his failure to do so.

Sweet said the central offence to which Hoffenberg pleaded guilty was a Ponzi scheme -- a fraudulent pyramid-type scheme that involves luring investors seeking high interest-rate returns and using the funds to pay off earlier investors.
Hoffenberg was accused of selling $450 million in fraudulent notes and bonds and using some funds from later investors to pay interest owed to earlier ones.
The rest of the money was used to run the Post for several months and to operate a financial empire with inflated revenues and profits that appeared to be a major health care financing company.

"The court has received hundreds of letters detailing the devastating economic, psychological and even physical effects of Hoffenberg's successful scheme to defraud over 3,000 individuals, companies, trust funds and pension plans," Sweet said.

The letters detailed the effects on "working people, the elderly, the disabled, single parents and their children, and police officers and firefighters whose lives were forever altered when their life savings, retirement and college funds were destroyed as a consequence of Hoffenberg's acts."

Sweet said that subject to Friday's hearing, he plans to sentence Hoffenberg to the prison term, followed by three years of probation, and order him to make restitution of $475.1 million and pay a fine of $1 million.
Victims of Hoffenberg's scheme have continued to suffer from financial frauds.
In July, a Los Angeles businessman who was supposed to help thousands of victims defrauded by Hoffenberg pleaded guilty to cheating the same investors.
The businessman, John Hall, formed the venture that took over the failed health-care financing and bill-collection business and was accused of siphoning off much of the company's assets.

Hall had been chief executive of Qualis Care, a venture formed in March 1994 by a partnership created by Hall and the Towers estate. His plan to take over Towers' assets was approved by a bankruptcy trustee in 1994, two years after Hall reached a settlement with securities regulators who had accused him of looting a small money-market fund.
